title: The Secrets of Hibernation
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: When winter comes, many animals face a crisis: the cold makes life uncomfortable, and food becomes hard to find. Some animals, such as swallows, solve the problem by migrating to a warmer region. Others stay and endure the cold by entering a state called hibernation, in which the body slows down so dramatically that it can survive for months on the fat stored during the summer. Hibernation is not simply a long sleep but a different state of life, with its own rules, its own dangers and its own surprising benefits.

During hibernation, an animal's body temperature, heart rate and breathing all fall. A ground squirrel's temperature may drop from about 37 degrees Celsius to just above freezing, and its heart rate from 200 beats a minute to as few as five. Its breathing may stop for several minutes at a time. These changes reduce the amount of energy that the animal uses to a few per cent of the normal figure, so that a small store of fat is enough to last the whole winter.

Not all hibernators behave in the same way. Some, like ground squirrels and bats, enter a deep state, and wake only every few weeks. Others, notably bears, enter a lighter state sometimes called torpor, in which the temperature falls by only five or six degrees. Female bears give birth in the middle of this period, in the den, without eating, drinking or passing waste, and they continue to feed their cubs on milk until spring. Scientists find this ability so remarkable that they study it for medical clues.

Preparing for hibernation takes months. In autumn, animals eat far more than usual, sometimes doubling their body weight, and they store the extra energy as fat. Some, such as chipmunks, also hide stores of food in their burrows and eat from them during their brief periods of waking. The animals must also choose a safe place. A good den or burrow has a steady temperature, protects from predators and stays dry; a poor choice can mean death, since a sleeper cannot escape from danger.

Why do hibernators wake up periodically if the state saves energy? The question puzzles scientists, because each awakening uses a great deal of energy, in total most of the energy that the animal spends during the winter. Some researchers believe that the animals need to sleep normally from time to time, since the brain still requires its ordinary rest. Others suggest that waking allows the body to repair damage or to remove waste. The truth is probably a combination of these explanations.

Hibernation is also a subject of medical research. Hibernating animals do not lose bone or muscle in the way that humans do after months in bed, and bears seem to avoid blood clots and kidney damage. Dr Elena Voss, a physiologist, hopes that understanding these mechanisms may one day help patients who must lie still for long periods, and perhaps even astronauts on long space journeys. Some researchers dream of putting humans into a state like hibernation, but that remains far from reality.

Climate change is complicating the lives of hibernators. In warmer winters, animals may wake early and find no food, or they may emerge to find that the plants on which they depend have not yet grown. Bats are also threatened by a disease called white-nose syndrome, caused by a fungus that grows on hibernating animals and makes them wake more often and use up their fat. Millions of bats have died in North America since the disease was first noticed in 2006, and scientists are searching for a cure.
